elements.reason: The abstract identifies the review as an 'integrative review' but does not identify the report as a 'systematic review' as required by the PRISMA Abstract checklist.

elements.quote: Through an integrative review, we aimed to identify approaches to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract includes an explicit statement of the main objective of the review.

elements.quote: Included studies were not restricted by research design; and had to evaluate the sustainability of an EBI in a healthcare context.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies key inclusion criteria (no restriction by design; must evaluate sustainability of EBIs in healthcare).
The abstract states only that a comprehensive search across five databases was applied but does not name the information sources or report when each source was last searched.

elements.quote: We assessed the methodological quality of studies using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to assess study methodological quality (MMAT), which addresses risk-of-bias/quality assessment methods.

elements.quote: Following Whittemore and Knafl's methodological process: (1) problem identification; (2) literature search; (3) data evaluation; (4) data analysis; and (5) presentation, a comprehensive search strategy was applied across five databases.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the methodological framework used for data evaluation, analysis, and presentation, indicating the approach to synthesize and present results.

elements.quote: Of 18,783 articles retrieved, 64 fit the inclusion criteria. Qualitative designs were most commonly used for evaluation (48%), with individual interviews as the predominant data collection method.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (64) and summarizes study characteristics (designs, data collection methods) but does not report the total number of participants.

elements.quote: Most studies (77%) did not measure sustainability outcomes, rather these studies focused on sustainability determinants.
elements.reason: The abstract presents findings relevant to the review question (proportion of studies measuring outcomes vs determinants) but does not present detailed results for main outcomes or participant counts per outcome.
No meta-analysis is reported in the abstract, so reporting a summary estimate and interval is not applicable.
The abstract does not report comparisons between groups, so indicating direction of effect and favored group is not applicable.
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision).

elements.quote: Our review offers methodological recommendations for sustainability evaluation research and highlights the importance in understanding mechanisms of sustainability to advance the field.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and states implications and recommendations.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide a register name or registration number.

elements.quote: Background: There is limited evidence to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) for healthcare improvement.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the current state of knowledge (limited evidence on sustainability evaluation of EBIs) establishing an important uncertainty that motivates the review.

elements.quote: As evaluation is necessary to determine effectiveness, this review aimed to improve our understanding of how the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare is evaluated. A focus on evaluation is what differentiates this review from recent syntheses published on approaches to sustainability research.
elements.reason: The paper explains the importance and need for the review—to improve understanding of sustainability evaluation and to address gaps in guidance on selecting theoretical approaches and measuring outcomes.

elements.quote: A focus on evaluation is what differentiates this review from recent syntheses published on approaches to sustainability research. We provide further insight by reporting when sustainability evaluations were performed (timing), and what methods, measures, and outcomes were reported in evaluations on the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly positions itself relative to existing syntheses and similar reviews, stating how it differs and builds on prior work.
This review is of evaluation approaches for sustainability rather than a review of intervention effects; no intervention mechanism of action is proposed or required for the review's objectives.

The review examines theoretical approaches and methods for evaluating sustainability rather than testing a specific complex intervention or presenting a logic model; no logic model is proposed or discussed as part of the review.

elements.quote: The aim of this integrative review was to identify and synthesize approaches that have been used to evaluate the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare. We aimed to enhance our understanding of sustainability definitions, research designs, data collection methods, timing, measures, and sustainability outcomes used for sustainability evaluation studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the review objective(s) in a question-style aim: to identify and synthesize approaches used to evaluate sustainability of EBIs and to enhance understanding of related elements (definitions, designs, methods, timing, measures, outcomes).

elements.quote: We conducted an integrative review that followed Whittemore and Knafl's [12] five-stage methodological process: (1) problem identification; (2) literature search; (3) data evaluation; (4) data analysis (data reduction, display, comparison, and conclusions); and (5) presentation. Integrative reviews can include diverse data sources and do not restrict the type of study design.
elements.reason: This review is an integrative review focused on evaluation approaches for sustainability of EBIs rather than a review of intervention effects; thus specifying planned comparisons using PICO is not applicable.

elements.quote: Articles were included if they: • Were published in a peer-review journal • Were primary research • Had explicit research design and data collection methods • Had an explicit theoretical ­ approach a for sustainability ­ (theory b , ­ model c , ­ framework d , ­ instrument e , method, checklist, process, strategy, conceptual- izations, development, pilot test and/or ­ tool f ) • Were within a healthcare ­ setting g • Evaluated the sustainability of an EBI (Note that inconsistent terminology for EBI is prominent and thus may be referred to as a QI intervention/ initia- tive in the literature).
elements.reason: Table 1 explicitly lists study characteristics used to determine eligibility including study type, design/data collection requirements, theoretical approach, setting, and that studies must evaluate sustainability of an EBI.

elements.quote: We only included published studies in the English language and peer-reviewed primary studies in this review. This review entailed a comprehensive search of published literature and rigorous review methods; however, we recognize that there is the possibility of incomplete retrieval of identified research. For example, all gray literature was excluded.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states report-level eligibility restrictions (published, English language, peer-reviewed primary studies) and that gray literature was excluded.
No explicit distinction was provided between excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding because outcome results were not reported.
The evidence describes variables extracted and inclusion groups but does not specify the groups used in each synthesis nor link them to comparisons defined in the review objectives.

elements.quote: We only included published studies in the English language and peer-reviewed primary studies in this review. This review entailed a comprehensive search of published literature and rigorous review methods; however, we recognize that there is the possibility of incomplete retrieval of identified research. For example, all gray literature was excluded.
elements.reason: The manuscript states notable restrictions (English language, published, peer-reviewed; exclusion of gray literature) and acknowledges potential incomplete retrieval, but does not provide a clear rationale explaining why these specific restrictions were imposed.

elements.quote: In December 2018 and July 2020, we searched the following databases: Ovid MEDLINE(R) and Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily (1946 to current); OVID Embase (1974 to current); EBSCOhost CINAHL Plus with Full-text (1937 to current); Wiley Cochrane Library (inception to current).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the dates when searches were conducted (December 2018 and July 2020) and lists the sources searched; supplementary info (text_24) further specifies Dec 21, 2018.

elements.quote: we searched the following databases: Ovid MEDLINE(R) and Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily (1946 to current); OVID Embase (1974 to current); EBSCOhost CINAHL Plus with Full-text (1937 to current); Wiley Cochrane Library (inception to current).

elements.quote: In the first screening stage, one reviewer (RF) independently screened the abstracts and titles of all the citations retrieved from the database searches. A second reviewer (AB) independently screened a randomly selected 10% of all titles and abstracts to verify selection for inclusion or exclusion. In the second stage, two reviewers (RF and AB) independently screened all full-text articles that had passed first-stage screening.
elements.reason: The text explicitly reports the number of reviewers at each stage: one primary screener for all titles/abstracts, a second reviewer screening a 10% sample, and two reviewers screening all full texts.

elements.quote: Table 3 Sustainability outcomes identified in included studies [6] Benefits for patients, staff, and stakeholders continue. Initiative activities or components of the intervention continue. Maintenance of relationships, partnerships, or networks. Maintenance of new procedures, and policies. Attention and awareness of the problem or issue is continued or increased. Replication, roll-out, or scale-up of the initiative. Capacity built within staff, stakeholders, and communities continues. Adaptation in response to new evidence or contextual influences. Gaining further funds to continue the initiative and maintain improvements.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists and defines nine specific sustainability outcome domains (Table 3) and describes sustainability outcomes across included studies.

elements.quote: Of 64 included studies, 66% ( n = 43) ... had a clear timing for evaluation and 33% ( n = 21) ... had unclear timing. Of the 43 studies with clear timing, 42% ( n = 18) evaluated sustainability at a single time point ... The remaining 57% ( n = 25) evaluated sustainability at multiple time points ... The majority of studies (63%; n = 40) conducted data collection post evaluation only ... Evaluation timing and data collection time points are provided in Table 9.
elements.reason: The paper reports overall timing of evaluations across studies (single vs multiple time points, pre/post) but does not specify the time frame of measurement for each listed outcome domain.
No statement was found indicating whether the authors sought all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g., all measures, time points, analyses) for included studies.
The manuscript does not describe a process for selecting among multiple compatible results within outcome domains (no methods reported for selecting specific measures/time points/analyses).
No changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance are reported in the manuscript; therefore reporting of such changes with rationales does not apply.

elements.quote: The two reviewers independently extracted the following variables: (1) study design, (2) evaluation type (independent versus composite), (3) sustainability definition and terms used, (4) type and name of theoretical approach, (5) purpose of approach use, (6) data collection methods, (7) timing of evaluation data collection (e.g., pre-, and/or post-implementation of intervention), (8) reported sustainability measures and, 9. reported sustainability outcomes.

elements.quote: Following Whittemore and Knafl's methodological process: (1) problem identification; (2) literature search; (3) data evaluation; (4) data analysis; and (5) presentation, a comprehensive search strategy was applied across five databases.

elements.quote: We used the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) [17] to assess the methodological quality of studies.
elements.reason: The MMAT tool is named, but no version or year of the MMAT is reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The MMAT [17] appraises the quality by study design type, such as quantitative, qualitative, or mixed empirical methods. We distinguished mixed-methods as studies combining both qualitative and quantitative methods, whereas studies classified as multi-methods used 2 + qualitative methods. The criteria are specific to each type of study, with five domains apportioned to qualitative studies and quantitative studies subdivided into randomized controlled, non-randomized and descriptive studies.
elements.reason: The domains/components and how they map to study designs (e.g., five domains for qualitative; quantitative subdivided into RCT, non-randomized, descriptive) are described.

elements.quote: Each study is assigned an overall quality score, using asterisks representing the quality appraisal of each study. Scores vary from 20% (*) when one criterion is met to 100% (*****) when all criteria are met.
elements.reason: An overall risk/quality score is reported and the scoring rules (percentage/asterisk scheme tied to number of criteria met) are described.
No information is provided about any adaptations made to the MMAT or other risk-of-bias tools in the supplied evidence.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool was used; the review used the established MMAT, so development/public accessibility of a new tool does not apply.

elements.quote: Two reviewers independently completed MMAT assessments and compared scoring.

No automation tools (use, training, performance, validation) for risk-of-bias assessment are mentioned in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: We extracted whether an included study evaluated (a) sustainability determinants and (b) sustainability outcomes and how they measured these variables. ...
